transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-05-25 14:00 PDT | Duration: ~60 mins | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Omar (Redwood SE), Jared (Brightlane Platform Lead), Lina (Brightlane Infra), Sara (CTO), Evan (Compliance)

00:00 Jared Patel: Okay, thanks everyone for joining, we are on for the weekly POC sync.
00:07 Maya Chen: Hey team, thanks for the time. Quick agenda: sizing review, autoscale options, burst tests, security calls. Is that good?
00:15 Sara Kim: Yep that's fine. We wanted to make sure the Dedicated sizing covers our intermittent spike patterns from our mobile app.
00:23 Omar Ruiz: Great. I pulled the telemetry you sent last week and sketched three candidate configs — a baseline pool for steady QPS, a burst buffer pool, and an emergency fallback.
00:35 Lina Gomez: Quick question — when you say "burst buffer pool" is that the Dedicated burst feature or is it just additional reserved instances?
00:42 Omar Ruiz: It's a mix. For Redwood Dedicated we recommend a small always-on reserved pool sized for 95th percentile steady throughput, plus an autoscale policy to spin up extra GPU nodes for sustained bursts, and a separate short-lived burst pool for sub-minute spikes.
00:58 Jared Patel: So like a baseline of N GPUs, autoscale up to M GPUs, and then a transient burst layer for <60s spikes?
01:05 Omar Ruiz: Exactly. And we configure policy for both CPU/GPU thresholds and request queue depth so we don't react to single-request variance.
01:15 Lina Gomez: How does KV cache play with the autoscale? Do we lose warm cache when nodes are torn down?
01:22 Omar Ruiz: Good question. The runtime keeps a distributed KV cache across the pool when using our Dedicated offering; when nodes are removed we do pre-eviction draining and optionally write back hot prefixes to a shared cache store. There's some tradeoff: more aggressive downscaling reduces cost but can increase token latency for cold requests.
01:41 Maya Chen: Which is why we recommend a policy with a cooldown window — say 3–5 minutes — and a warm node buffer so cache churn is minimized.
01:50 Sara Kim: We care about 95th pct latency under 250ms for single-turn completions and p95 under 500ms for chat. Do you think the baseline pool alone can hit that?
01:59 Omar Ruiz: Baseline sized to the 95th should, yes. But in our early runs we saw 95th jump during the morning push. That's where the burst pool helps — it keeps latency under the SLO while autoscale fills the mid-range.
02:14 Jared Patel: Can you walk through the numbers you used? I want to compare to our internal calc.
02:18 Omar Ruiz: Sure — using your avg token length and calls per second data, baseline of 4x A100-equivalent GPUs for steady 120 QPS, autoscale policy up to 12 GPUs for sustained 10-minute >200 QPS, plus a burst buffer of 4 GPUs that can be tapped for sub-minute spikes. Cost estimates are in the sheet I updated.
02:40 Lina Gomez: A100-equivalent — we actually run on Ampere nodes for infra, our cloud partner is on A10G — does that materially change sizing?
02:48 Omar Ruiz: It shifts perf per GPU. The spreadsheet includes a perf factor table; we can swap in A10G numbers. The important part is the request latency curves and KV cache hit rate assumptions.
03:00 Sara Kim: During last week's test we saw tail latencies spike to 1.2s for some chat scenarios. What caused that?
03:06 Omar Ruiz: From logs it looked like cold KV cache misses combined with a short-lived fanout when multiple requests for the same prefix arrived during scale-up. We're proposing two mitigations: pre-warm high-frequency prefixes and set a slightly longer scale-up ramp so we don't trigger many small nodes rapidly.
03:23 Jared Patel: Pre-warm how — via synthetic traffic or background prefetch?
03:27 Omar Ruiz: Both options — you can run a background prefetch job for known hot prompts, or inject a small synthetic traffic during expected peak windows. We documented both in the runbook link in the sheet.
03:39 Evan Ross: On security, a couple items — KMS key rotation, audit log retention (we need 7 years), and evidence of SOC2 controls.
03:48 Maya Chen: We can share our security packet; Redwood Private has options for customer-managed KMS and extended audit retention as an add-on. For Dedicated, we support KMS integration and detailed audit logs — we'll include a sample retention policy in the docs.
04:03 Evan Ross: Also need to confirm whether audit logs can be forwarded to our SIEM in real time.
04:07 Omar Ruiz: Yes, we can forward logs via syslog/HTTPS to your Splunk/Datadog. There's a config for log push frequency — we'll include recommended settings.
04:18 Sara Kim: Back to autoscale: what about cooldowns — you suggested 3–5 minutes. Can we do 10 minutes to avoid flapping?
04:25 Omar Ruiz: You can. Longer cooldown reduces cost variability by avoiding oscillation but increases risk of sustained higher latency during intermediate drops. With a separate burst buffer we found 5–7 minutes is a good balance. If you prefer 10 we can size baseline slightly higher to compensate.
04:40 Jared Patel: Let's try 7 minutes initially. Also want to run two burst scenarios: short high QPS spikes (30–45s) and longer medium spikes (5–12 minutes).
04:50 Maya Chen: That matches our recommendations. Action: we'll update the sheet with those two burst cases and estimated spin-up times and cost delta.
04:58 Lina Gomez: One more infra question — network egress and multi-AZ distribution. If we autoscale across AZs how does KV cache locality work?
05:06 Omar Ruiz: Our runtime prefers local-AZ placement for KV hot prefixes, and cross-AZ reads are allowed but with a small added latency. For multi-AZ autoscale we recommend partitioning hot prefixes by region or enabling cross-AZ cache replication for critical prefixes. There is some cost for replication.
05:22 Sara Kim: Could you share numbers for cross-AZ penalty?
05:25 Omar Ruiz: Typically 10–40ms added per token depending on region pairing; it's in the perf appendix of the spreadsheet.
05:34 Jared Patel: For the burst test, we'll provide a sample of our real request traces for the peak hour. Can you consume that trace to run an accurate replay?
05:41 Omar Ruiz: Yes, we can ingest your trace format (we support JMeter and custom JSON). Please obfuscate any PHI before sending.
05:47 Evan Ross: Important — PHI must be removed or use a synthetic replay.
05:50 Lina Gomez: We'll scrub names and PII.
05:53 Omar Ruiz: Thanks. For the run we'll do two runs: 30-min steady at 1.5x peak, then 10 short bursts 30–60s at 3x peak to mimic flash events. We'll capture token latency, queue depth, and node spin-up time.
06:10 Maya Chen: I'll update the sheet and post a link in the follow-up. Also sharing the recommended autoscale YAML snippets so Lina can feed them into infra.
06:18 Jared Patel: Any concerns on cost for Dedicated? We need to present to finance.
06:22 Maya Chen: We included cost deltas for baseline vs autoscale vs burst buffer. The sheet has cost per hour and monthly estimate assuming your traffic shape. For 4 baseline GPUs + average autoscale to 8 GPUs, the delta is X — see sheet.
06:36 Sara Kim: Can you include comms on cold start cost for chat sessions? We want to see worst-case monthly compute overhead.
06:42 Omar Ruiz: We'll add a worst-case estimate assuming zero shared cache and 20% cold requests.
06:48 Jared Patel: Sounds good. On next steps, let's run the test next week and then meet for results review.
06:55 Maya Chen: Confirmed. We'll run tests starting 2026-06-01 and sync the week of 2026-06-08.
07:01 Evan Ross: I'll set up a security-specific call after you share the packet.
07:05 Maya Chen: Great — recap of action items in the doc. Anything else?
07:09 Sara Kim: No, that's it. Thanks.
07:12 Maya Chen: Thanks all, bye.

End of transcript. Notes: transcription contains occasional mis-heard words (KV cash / Dedicate) in the raw export; timestamps are approximate. Links referenced: sizing spreadsheet (https://redwood.app/s/poc-sizing-Brightlane), autoscale runbook (https://redwood.app/r/autoscale-runbook)
